introduction: These hundred readings put love at the foundation of everything: the cause of creation, the first sign of faith, the one thing in religion that never changes, the bond that holds atoms and societies together, and the fruit a human life is meant to bear. I loved thy creation, hence I created thee, says one; when love appears all books are rolled up, says another. Beside them stand the great statements of love in other scriptures and in poets and philosophers, from the commandments of Leviticus and the Gospels and Paul's hymn to charity to the Song of Songs, the Dhammapada, Sa‘di, Dante and Augustine. Other voices ask whether love can bear so much weight: Machiavelli and Hobbes on fear and power, Tennyson on nature red in tooth and claw, Heraclitus on strife, the Buddhist counsel to love nothing, Dostoevsky on loving mankind and not one's neighbour.
questions: The readings say the world was created through love. What in your experience of the world supports that, and what, like Tennyson's nature, cries out against it?
Machiavelli thought it safer to be feared than loved, and Hobbes that order rests on power. Where have you seen love do what fear could not, and the reverse?
One reading says that many who hate each other heartily profess friendship. How is love without dissimulation recognized?
The Dhammapada advises loving nothing so as to lose nothing. What do the readings say is worth the pain?
Dostoevsky's character loves humanity and cannot stand people. Who is the one difficult person through whom your love of humankind is tested?
A reading asks that we see every human being as a letter from the Beloved, however blotted. What would change in a single day if you did?

outside.why: Dante ends his poem with the Love which moves the sun and the other stars.
The first letter of John says that love is of God, and that God is love.
Jesus named two commandments on which hang all the law and the prophets: love of God and love of neighbour.
The first letter of John asks how one who loves not his brother whom he has seen can love God whom he has not seen.
Sa‘di wrote that the sons of Adam are limbs of each other, having been created of one essence.
Paul says: now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
Paul tells the Galatians that they have been called unto liberty, and asks them by love to serve one another.
Machiavelli asked whether it is better to be loved than feared, and answered that it is much safer to be feared. Is love a sound first principle for dealing with people as they are?
Paul asks the Romans: let love be without dissimulation; be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love.
Hamlet writes it down as a discovery that one may smile, and smile, and be a villain.
Spinoza wrote that hatred is increased by being reciprocated, and can on the other hand be destroyed by love.
The Dhammapada says: hatred does not cease by hatred at any time; hatred ceases by love; this is an old rule.
Jesus taught: love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you.
In the parable it is a stranger, a Samaritan, who has compassion on the wounded man.
Paul says that love worketh no ill to his neighbour; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.
Jesus said: a new commandment I give unto you, that ye love one another.
The Qur’an says that for those who believe and do good works the Beneficent will appoint love.
Hillel said: that which is hateful to you do not do to another; that is the entire Torah.
Hobbes held that where there is no common power there is no law, and where no law, no injustice. Is a body politic held together by love, or by a power all must fear?

Darwin wrote that as civilisation advances reason tells each person to extend his sympathies to all the members of the same nation, and then to all nations. Is the widening of love a law of history or a gift of religion?
Isaiah foresees nations beating their swords into plowshares, and learning war no more.
In John's Gospel Jesus prays for all who will believe: that they all may be one.
Jesus said: by this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
The first letter of John says: we know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren.
The Song of Songs says that love is strong as death, and the coals thereof are coals of fire.
Paul lists the fruit of the Spirit, and love comes first: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness.
Through Jeremiah God says: I have loved thee with an everlasting love.
The first letter of John says: we love him, because he first loved us.
In Hosea God says: I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love.
In Isaiah God says: can a woman forget her sucking child? Yet will I not forget thee; I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands.
Augustine says to God: You have made us for Yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in You.
Julian of Norwich was told: wouldst thou learn thy Lord's meaning in this thing? Love was His meaning.
Spinoza wrote that he who loves God cannot endeavour that God should love him in return. Is love for God a response to being loved, or something that asks no return?
John's Gospel says: God so loved the world, that He gave His only begotten Son.
Plato describes love as an ascent, from beautiful things step by step to a nature of wondrous beauty. Is love the cause of creation, or the creature's way back?
The first letter of John says: if we love one another, God dwelleth in us, and His love is perfected in us.
Paul says that charity suffereth long, and is kind; beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
Thomas à Kempis says that love is a great thing, which alone makes every heavy thing light.
The Letter to the Colossians says: above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.
Paul prays that his friends, rooted and grounded in love, may know the love which passeth knowledge.
The Song of Songs says that many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.

Tennyson wrote of one who trusted that love was creation's final law, though Nature, red in tooth and claw, shrieked against his creed. What in the world as you see it supports that trust, and what tells against it?
Shelley wrote that nothing in the world is single; all things by a law divine in one spirit meet and mingle.
The beloved in the Song of Songs says: his banner over me was love.
Plato's Socrates calls the madness of love the greatest of heaven's blessings. Why would the greatest sign also be an affliction?
The Dhammapada concludes from the pain of losing what is loved that one should love nothing. What is the answer to the charge that love is the root of suffering?
Paul says that though he speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, he is become as sounding brass.
The Qur’an says that mankind have broken their religion among them into sects, each group rejoicing in its tenets.
Augustine found three things in love: he that loves, and that which is loved, and love.
Augustine wrote that two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, the heavenly by the love of God. How many kinds of love are there, and are all of them love?
The Qur’an bids its Prophet say: if ye love God, follow me; God will love you.
Paul is persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the love of God.
Paul says that we, beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image.
Boethius wrote in prison that all things are seen to yearn, in due time, for due return.
Heraclitus said that war is the father of all and the king of all. Is it attraction or strife that moves the world?
The Letter to the Colossians says of the creating Word: by him all things consist.
Whitman wrote that whoever walks a furlong without sympathy walks to his own funeral dressed in his shroud.
Paul says that the body is one and hath many members, and all the members are one body.
Paul says that though he give his body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth him nothing. What is missing from a good act done without love?
Proverbs says: better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
Nelson Mandela wrote that love comes more naturally to the human heart than its opposite.
The first words every Jewish child learns join the oneness of God to a command to love Him.
The first letter of Peter says: above all things have fervent charity among yourselves.
In John's Gospel Jesus says it in seven words: if ye love me, keep my commandments.
Augustine gave a short precept once for all: love, and do what you will.
Jesus distinguished the tithing of herbs from the weightier matters of the law: judgment, mercy and faith.
Leviticus gives the commandment in its oldest form: thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
Genesis has God say: let us make man in our image, after our likeness.
Asked by a disciple about benevolence, Confucius said: it is to love all men.
Pope wrote that in faith and hope the world will disagree, but all mankind's concern is charity. If love is the common ground of all, what do the religions add?
Aristotle said that man, when perfected, is the best of animals, but separated from law and justice the worst. Is love or law what makes the human world human?
Shakespeare wrote that love is not love which alters when it alteration finds; it is an ever-fixed mark. How is the love that lasts told from the kind that passes?
The disciples at Emmaus asked: did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?
Blake wrote that we are put on earth a little space that we may learn to bear the beams of love.
Jesus said: he that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. Does love of God take from other loves, or give them their place?
Proverbs says that a friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
Montaigne could explain his love for his friend only by saying: because it was he, because it was I.
Jesus said: I am come to send fire on the earth, and what will I, if it be already kindled?
The psalm says: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
Jesus washed his disciples' feet and said: ye also ought to wash one another's feet.
The Letter to the Ephesians says: speak every man truth with his neighbour, for we are members one of another.
Proverbs says that hatred stirreth up strifes, but love covereth all sins.
Ruth said: intreat me not to leave thee; whither thou goest, I will go, and thy people shall be my people.
Emerson wrote that a friend is a person with whom I may be sincere; before him I may think aloud.
Jesus told of a merchant who found one pearl of great price, and sold all that he had, and bought it.
Whitman found letters from God dropped in the street, every one signed by God's name.
In the parable the King says: inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
A character in Dostoevsky confesses: the more I love humanity in general, the less I love man in particular. Why is it harder to love one difficult person than all mankind?
Proverbs says that open rebuke is better than secret love. What does love owe to someone besides warmth?
Jesus said: I am the vine, ye are the branches; he that abideth in me bringeth forth much fruit.
Jesus said: be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.
Jesus said: ye shall know them by their fruits; do men gather grapes of thorns?
The first psalm likens the blessed man to a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season.
The Preacher says that of making many books there is no end.
Rumi's reed-flute tells its story of longing without a book: I burst my breast, striving to give vent to sighs.
The Qur’an says to its Prophet: We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples.
John Donne wrote that any man's death diminishes him, because he is involved in mankind.
The first letter to Timothy says that the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart.
Jesus said: think not that I am come to send peace on earth; I came not to send peace, but a sword. How is that saying to be read beside the claim that every prophet brought only the message of love?
Jesus said: greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.

john-god-so-loved-the-world.text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life

jeremiah-everlasting-love.text: Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee

john-epistle-perfect-love-casteth-out-fe.text: There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love. We love him, because he first loved us

ephesians-rooted-and-grounded-in-love.text: that ye, being rooted and grounded in love, May be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height; And to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge, that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God

colossians-bond-of-perfectness.text: And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness

hosea-cords-of-a-man.text: I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love

romans-love-without-dissimulation.text: Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good. Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another

psalm-smoother-than-butter.text: The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords

john-epistle-love-one-another.text: Beloved, if God so loved us, we ought also to love one another. No man hath seen God at any time. If we love one another, God dwelleth in us, and his love is perfected in us

song-banner-over-me-was-love.text: He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love

proverbs-open-rebuke.text: Open rebuke is better than secret love

dhammapada-hatred-ceases-by-love.text: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule
